html:
The Nambikwara are an Indigenous people of western Mato Grosso and Rondônia in Brazil, living on the dry upland savannas between the Guaporé and Juruena rivers. About 1,150 live in their territories today.

They moved between dry season camps, where they hunted and gathered, and rainy season villages with gardens. In 1907 the telegraph line of Cândido Rondon crossed their land, and contact brought measles and influenza. In 1938 the French anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss lived among them, and wrote about them in his book Tristes Tropiques. Their neighbours include the Arawakan Paresi and the Enawenê-nawê.
